Both answers say their sources have nothing on this and guess that Tan would say ownership matters. B leans more on Paul Graham's views as a stand-in and on the generic point that the employer usually owns the work, which is the generic trap.

Both reach the right conclusion: don't build every request, cut down and launch now. The Seibel quotes I checked are real, but both answers miss Dalton's StandardDB story about deleting 80% of features and the warning against piping user-call notes into an AI to build everything. B wins narrowly: it says outright that cheap AI building makes the trap worse, and it gives a clearer rule for which requested features belong in the launch.

Both answers get Seibel's core point: stop paying lawyers to fight over pre-PMF stock that is worth almost nothing. Neither gives his specifics (cut the departing founder to under 5%, or under 2% in year one; generous severance; about a week and $2,000). I prefer A because it says a large vested stake held by a departed founder is dead equity that should shrink, which is close to Seibel's view. B suggests the departing founder simply keeps what has vested, which is the generic trap and the opposite of his advice.

Both answers say plainly that they have no Tan source material and both miss his actual plan: the markdown library, skill files, recurring jobs, 'skillify', and the warning that most people quit in week two. A comes closer because its concrete day-by-day week starts with installing a coding agent like Claude Code, which matches his 'pick a harness tonight' step. B stays more general.

Both answers miss PG's actual position. Both answers also wrongly claim the sources have nothing on agents, even though web-19ac0b6d18d2 covers it. Their general quotes are real.
